title: US classification levels: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential
t: US classification levels: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential
description:
The US classifies national-security information at three levels: Confidential (damage), Secret (serious damage), Top Secret (exceptionally grave damage) — plus handling caveats like SCI and SAP. EO 13526 (2009) governs the system; only the damage standard justifies classification.

The levels are public knowledge; the classified contents are not. This record documents the system.

title: The UK classification system
description:
The UK's Government Security Classifications — Official, Secret, Top Secret — replaced the old five-tier system in 2014. Most government business is 'Official'; the higher tiers protect genuinely sensitive material.

The framework is public policy; the protected contents are not.

title: Classification systems worldwide
description:
Most nations run parallel systems — France's Tres Secret, Russia's classifications, China's state-secrets law — each with public frameworks and secret contents. NATO's COSMIC Top Secret coordinates allied sharing.

Comparing the public frameworks shows a shared logic: damage-based tiers, need-to-know, and declassification schedules.

title: The Wassenaar Arrangement (1996)
description:
The Wassenaar Arrangement — 42 participating states — coordinates export controls on conventional arms and dual-use goods and technologies. Its public control lists name the categories: electronics, computers, telecoms, sensors, navigation, marine, aerospace.

The lists are public; the controlled items' details are commercial, not secret.

description:

Math was a weapon, then wasn't — by public rulemaking.

title: How restriction categories are published
description:
Restriction categories reach the public through the Federal Register, agency regulations, public lists (SDN, CCL, USML), and international treaties. This database is built from exactly these sources.

The restrictions that matter are the published ones.

title: Licenses and exceptions
description:
Every restriction regime has licenses, exceptions, and grandfather clauses — the law's safety valves. License applications, general licenses, and published guidance are public.

Restriction is rarely absolute; the exceptions are part of the system.
